# What this document is

In labs 01, 02 and 03a you ran code that was written for you and interpreted the
output. **Here you write the code.**

There are two tasks. Both are open-ended: there is no single correct answer, and
different groups will get genuinely different results. That is the point — we
will compare across groups at the end of the session.

Fill in the chunks marked `# TODO`. Keep your interpretation in the prose

## Setup

This is given to you — run it and move on.

```{r libraries}
library(MOFA2)
library(mixOmics)
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r data}
data(breast.TCGA)

X <- list(
  mirna   = breast.TCGA$data.train$mirna,
  mrna    = breast.TCGA$data.train$mrna,
  protein = breast.TCGA$data.train$protein
)
subtype <- breast.TCGA$data.train$subtype

# Clinical annotation, joined on the short TCGA sample barcode.
# NOTE: TCGA writes missing values as the literal string '-- , so we declare it
# as NA on read. Leave that out and you get a spurious extra category.
clinical <- read_tsv("../data/TCGA-BRCA.Clinical.tsv",
                     na = c("", "NA", "'--"),
                     name_repair = "unique_quiet",
                     col_types = cols(age_at_index = "i", .default = "c")) |>
  select(case_submitter_id, age_at_index, ethnicity, vital_status,
         ajcc_pathologic_stage, primary_diagnosis) |>
  mutate(
    SampleID = gsub("TCGA-([A-Z0-9]+)-(.*)", "\\2", case_submitter_id),
    # ajcc_pathologic_stage has 9 levels, several with <5 samples. This coarser
    # version is often the more useful one -- your choice which you use.
    stage_coarse = str_extract(ajcc_pathologic_stage, "Stage (I{1,3}V?|IV|X)")
  ) |>
  distinct_all()

candidate_covariates <- c("age_at_index", "ethnicity", "vital_status",
                          "stage_coarse", "primary_diagnosis")

lapply(X, dim)
```

How many samples you actually have per group matters for every test you are
about to run. **Check before you choose**, and come back to this table when you
interpret a result:

```{r covariate-counts}
tibble(sample = rownames(X$mrna)) |>
  left_join(clinical, by = join_by(sample == SampleID)) |>
  select(all_of(candidate_covariates)) |>
  map(~ table(.x, useNA = "ifany"))
```

A small helper so you are not writing boilerplate every time you want a model.
`views` lets you fit on a subset of the omics — you will need that in task 2.

```{r fit-helper}
fit_mofa <- function(views = names(X), num_factors = 10, seed = 42) {
  obj <- create_mofa(lapply(X[views], t))

  data_opts  <- get_default_data_options(obj)
  data_opts$scale_views <- TRUE

  model_opts <- get_default_model_options(obj)
  model_opts$num_factors <- num_factors

  train_opts <- get_default_training_options(obj)
  train_opts$convergence_mode <- "fast"   # "slow" for a final model
  train_opts$seed    <- seed
  train_opts$verbose <- FALSE

  obj <- prepare_mofa(obj,
    data_options     = data_opts,
    model_options    = model_opts,
    training_options = train_opts
  )
  obj <- run_mofa(obj, outfile = tempfile(fileext = ".hdf5"),
                  use_basilisk = FALSE)

  # Attach subtype and the clinical columns to the model's sample metadata.
  samples_metadata(obj) <- samples_metadata(obj) |>
    mutate(Subtype = subtype) |>
    left_join(clinical, by = join_by(sample == SampleID))

  obj
}
```

```{r fit-full}
mofa_full <- fit_mofa()
mofa_full
```

Every group takes a **different** covariate:

|---|---|
| `age_at_index` | continuous |
| `ethnicity` | categorical |
| `vital_status` | categorical |
| `stage_coarse` (or `ajcc_pathologic_stage`) | categorical |
| `primary_diagnosis` | categorical |

Do **not** use `Subtype` — lab 03a already did, and it dominates everything.

## 1a. Which factors relate to your covariate?

Run the association test across **all** the candidate covariates at once, then
find yours in the result.

> Two things you need to know, because they will bite you otherwise:
>
> 1. `correlate_factors_with_covariates()` clusters the rows of its heatmap, so
>    it **errors if you pass only one covariate**. Pass the whole set
>    (`candidate_covariates` is already defined for you).
> 2. It warns that it is *converting non-numeric values to numeric*. For a
>    categorical covariate with more than two unordered levels that is
>    statistically wrong — it treats your categories as though they sat on a
>    numeric scale. We deal with that in 1b.

## 1b. Test your covariate properly

Because of the numeric coercion above, write your own test of your covariate
against each factor.

> Hint: `get_factors(mofa_full)[[1]]` gives you the samples × factors matrix.
> For a **categorical** covariate use `kruskal.test(values ~ groups)`; for a
> **continuous** one use `cor.test(..., method = "spearman")`.
> `apply(Z, 2, ...)` runs your test down every factor. Watch out for `NA`s.


You just ran one test per factor. **Does your best p-value survive a Bonferroni

## 2c. Compare how well each model separates the subtypes

This is the part that actually answers "was it worth it". For each model, show
whether the factors still separate the three subtypes (Basal, Her2, LumA).

Pick your own approach. Two reasonable ones:

- **Visual:** `plot_factors()` on the top two factors, coloured by `Subtype`,
  for each model side by side.
- **Quantitative:** for each model, test each factor against `Subtype` with
  `kruskal.test` and keep the best p-value — or fit a classifier on the factors
  and report cross-validated accuracy.

The quantitative route makes for a much stronger answer.
